---

# SEC Filing Analysis: HPS Corporate Lending Fund (HLEND) — 8-K / April 14, 2026

---

## A. Relevance Verdict

**HIGHLY RELEVANT TO PRIVATE CREDIT**

This filing drops a single, concrete fundraising data point — April 1 subscriptions of $151 million — into a charged environment where HLEND triggered a landmark redemption gate just five weeks earlier. The number matters precisely because of what came before it.

---

## B. One-Line Takeaway

HLEND discloses $151M in April 1, 2026 subscriptions — the first fresh inflow figure since the fund gated Q1 2026 redemptions at its 5% quarterly cap after investors demanded back 9.3% of assets.

---

## C. What's New

- **New subscription figure disclosed:** As of Feb. 28, 2026, the fund reported more than $4.4 billion in available liquidity and said it had raised approximately $840 million in new subscriptions during the first quarter of 2026. The April 14 8-K now adds a fresh data point: **$151.0 million in net proceeds from subscriptions effective April 1, 2026** — the first subscription date of Q2 2026, and the first since the gating event.

- **Post-gating fundraising signal:** The $151M April 1 subscription figure is the earliest observable inflow data since HLEND capped investor withdrawals after redemption requests exceeded the fund's quarterly liquidity limit for the first time since launch — with repurchase requests for Q1 2026 totaling 9.3% of outstanding shares, nearly double the established 5% quarterly cap.

- **Reg FD disclosure timed to BlackRock earnings call:** The 8-K states the information was disclosed during the **BlackRock, Inc. investor conference call on April 14, 2026** — meaning this is coordinated investor messaging, not a standalone filing.

- **Multi-class share issuance confirmed:** The April 1 subscriptions spanned Class I, Class D, Class F, and Class S shares simultaneously — confirming the retail wealth channel remains active across all distribution tiers.

- **No routine net-subscription disclosures existed prior for individual dates:** HLEND historically aggregates subscription data by quarter. Disclosing a single monthly subscription date figure under Reg FD, tied to a BlackRock earnings call, is a deliberate transparency signal — or damage control.

---

## D. Most Important Points

- **$151.0 million** in net subscription proceeds effective **April 1, 2026** — the first subscription date following the Q1 2026 redemption gate.

- For context: HLEND had raised approximately $840 million in new subscriptions during the first quarter of 2026 — spread across three monthly subscription dates (January 1, February 1, March 1). That implies a Q1 monthly average of roughly **$280 million per subscription date**. The April 1 figure of $151M is approximately **46% below that average**.

- The $26 billion fund — one of the largest non-traded BDCs — saw shareholders request 9.3% of their shares in Q1; management capped repurchases at 5%, and while the total value would have been about $1.2 billion, investors received back about $620 million.

- HLEND's board approved repurchases of 5% of shares outstanding, amounting to roughly $620 million. The $151M April subscription alone does not offset the $620M payout, let alone the unfulfilled ~$580M in redemption requests.

- HLEND is a private credit fund managed by HPS Investment Partners, LLC, part of BlackRock. This makes any fundraising signal a public event for BlackRock, a listed company.

- BlackRock Inc., which completed its acquisition of HPS Investment Partners in July 2025, saw its shares fall nearly 7% in afternoon trading following the gating announcement.

- HLEND is a public, perpetually non-traded BDC that seeks to deliver attractive risk-adjusted returns, primarily in the form of current income, by investing in a diversified, high-quality portfolio of predominantly senior secured, floating-rate, privately originated loans to middle and upper-middle market companies.

- The fund is committed to delivering quarterly liquidity up to 5% of fund shares. That structural limit is now in the spotlight after being triggered.

- Private credit funds broadly are bracing for a wave of redemption requests as angst grows around the industry's lending practices and exposure to businesses that could be upended by artificial intelligence.

- The 8-K is filed under **Item 7.01 (Regulation FD Disclosure)** — meaning it is furnished, not filed, and was communicated orally at the BlackRock earnings call first. This signals management wanted the number on the record immediately.

---

## E. Why It Matters Now

BlackRock curbed withdrawals from one of its biggest private credit funds after client requests for redemptions spiked — the latest sign of investor anxiety about the $1.8 trillion private credit industry. The April 14 8-K provides the first hard data point on whether new investor capital is still flowing into HLEND post-gating. At $151M for the April 1 subscription date — roughly half the Q1 monthly average — inflows appear to have decelerated materially, though one data point does not establish a trend. The redemption request news came amid growing apprehensions about systemic risks in the private credit market; Blackstone raised its redemption cap from 5% to 7% after facing a surge of requests; Blue Owl moved to restrict investor withdrawals from a retail-focused fund; and Apollo's CEO has warned that a shakeout is coming for private credit firms, including concerns about rising defaults on loans to software companies. The fundraising slowdown — if confirmed across May and June subscription dates — would compound the liquidity picture at one of the sector's most prominent retail-facing private credit vehicles.

---

## F. Filing Details Extracted

| **Filer** | HPS Corporate Lending Fund |

| **Interest-rate / spread terms** | Not disclosed in this filing |
| **Key covenant or amendment terms** | Not disclosed in this filing |

| **Watchlist entity match** | **Yes** — HLEND triggered its 5% quarterly redemption cap in Q1 2026, a high-profile gating event that moved BlackRock's stock price |

---

## G. Signals Reporters Should Notice

- **Post-gating subscription deceleration:** $151M on April 1 is the first hard number after gating. If May and June subscription dates are also lower, HLEND's net asset growth stalls at exactly the wrong moment — when ~$580M in unfulfilled Q1 redemption requests may roll into Q2.

- **Coordinated messaging with BlackRock earnings call:** Disclosing a single subscription-date figure via Reg FD 8-K timed to the BlackRock investor call signals management is managing the optics around fundraising health. This is not standard reporting practice for HLEND.

- **Negative net flow risk:** The board approved repurchases of approximately $620 million in Q1. If Q2 subscriptions continue at $151M/month, one quarter of inflows (~$450M) would not cover a repeat gating scenario of similar size.

- **Retail wealth channel vulnerability:** The gating highlights a structural feature of retail-focused private credit vehicles: periodic liquidity limits designed to align investor capital with the longer duration of private loans — and when withdrawal requests exceed those limits, funds typically prorate repurchases or cap them at preset thresholds. HLEND's retail distribution model is now under scrutiny.

- **BlackRock's reputation exposure:** BlackRock agreed to acquire HPS in a roughly $12 billion transaction as part of a broader push into private lending, a business that has ballooned to an estimated $3 trillion in assets. Any sustained fundraising weakness at HLEND directly tests the strategic rationale of that deal.

---

## H. Routine vs. Non-Routine

**Routine / expected:**
- Reg FD 8-K disclosures for subscription data are procedurally standard for non-traded BDCs
- Monthly share issuances across Class I, D, F, and S are part of HLEND's normal operating structure
- Linking a disclosure to an earnings call is common practice for fund sponsors post-acquisition

**Potentially non-routine / notable:**
- Disclosing a *single* subscription date figure (rather than waiting for quarterly aggregate) is atypical and likely driven by investor relations pressure post-gating
- $151M is materially below the Q1 monthly average of ~$280M, suggesting a discernible slowdown in inflows
- The timing — exactly 39 days after the gating announcement — makes this the de facto "first read" on whether the gating event spooked new investors
- The BlackRock investor call on the same date as the filing suggests the number was flagged in prepared remarks, making it worth reviewing the full earnings transcript for management commentary around HLEND fundraising

---

## I. Questions for Follow-Up

1. **What was the May 1 and June 1 subscription amount?** Is April's $151M a one-month dip or the beginning of a sustained fundraising slowdown?

2. **What did BlackRock management say about HLEND fundraising on the April 14 investor call?** Did they frame $151M as stabilization, recovery, or did they avoid direct comparison to Q1?

3. **How many of the unfulfilled Q1 redemption requests (~$580M) rolled into Q2?** Could Q2 redemption volume again approach or exceed the 5% cap?

4. **What is the net flow picture?** If Q2 subscriptions run at $151M/month (~$450M/quarter) and redemptions are again capped at $620M, HLEND would be in negative net flow for Q2.

5. **Is HLEND deploying capital faster or slower post-gating?** Lower inflows may constrain new originations, affecting yield and performance in subsequent quarters.

6. **Are financial advisors pulling back on recommending HLEND to clients?** The retail distribution channel is the fund's primary growth engine — any advisor hesitancy would structurally impair fundraising.

7. **How does $151M compare to subscription levels at HLEND's peer BDCs** (e.g., Blue Owl's BDCs, Ares Capital, Blackstone Credit) for the same period?

8. **Has the fund disclosed any change in its tender offer terms or quarterly liquidity cap in response to Q1 events?** Any amendment to the 5% cap — up or down — would be a major signal.

---

## J. Evidence from the Filing

**From Item 7.01 (the only substantive disclosure in the 8-K):**

> *"As discussed during the investor conference call of BlackRock, Inc. on April 14, 2026, HPS Corporate Lending Fund ('HLEND' or the 'Fund') received $151.0 million of net proceeds relating to the issuance of Class I shares, Class D shares, Class F shares and Class S shares for subscriptions effective April 1, 2026."*

This is the entirety of the substantive new information in the filing. The rest is boilerplate corporate identity data, XBRL taxonomy extensions, and standard Reg FD furnishing language. There are no exhibits containing additional financial data, portfolio updates, or risk disclosures.

**Inferred from filing context (not stated in filing):**
- The deliberate brevity of this 8-K, combined with its same-day timing to the BlackRock earnings call, implies the number was likely disclosed verbally first and the 8-K was filed immediately to satisfy Reg FD compliance.
- The CFO, **Robert Busch**, signed the filing, consistent with standard practice.

---

## K. Final Newsroom Brief

**INTERNAL ALERT — HLEND / April 14, 2026**

HPS Corporate Lending Fund filed an 8-K today disclosing $151.0 million in net subscription proceeds for the April 1, 2026 subscription date — the first fresh inflow figure since the fund triggered its 5% quarterly redemption cap in March 2026, one of the most high-profile gating events in the retail private credit market to date. The $26 billion fund — one of the largest non-traded BDCs — saw shareholders request 9.3% of shares in Q1, but management capped repurchases at 5%. The April figure of $151M is roughly half of the fund's Q1 2026 monthly subscription average of approximately $280M, suggesting a meaningful deceleration in new investor capital — though one month does not confirm a trend. The disclosure was timed to and referenced during the BlackRock investor conference call today, signaling management is actively managing fundraising optics. Private credit funds broadly are bracing for a wave of redemption requests as investor anxiety about the industry's lending practices grows, and HLEND's post-gating inflow trajectory is now one of the most closely watched data series in the sector. Reporters should seek the May and June subscription figures and review the full BlackRock earnings call transcript for management commentary on HLEND fundraising velocity and any update on Q2 redemption request levels.

---
*Analysis based on SEC filing 0001628280-26-024994 and public context as of April 14, 2026. Dollar comparisons to Q1 2026 monthly averages are analyst inference, not stated in the filing. Treat the fundraising deceleration signal as preliminary pending additional monthly data points.*

---

## SEC Filing Analysis: StepStone Private Credit Fund LLC — 8-K / April 10, 2026

---

### A. Relevance Verdict

**POSSIBLY RELEVANT TO PRIVATE CREDIT**

The filing discloses the clean termination of a $250M insurance-capital-backed SPV facility for a growing private credit BDC. It is structurally relevant to the private credit ecosystem but does not signal distress, default, or immediate newsworthy stress.

---

### B. One-Line Takeaway

StepStone Private Credit Fund LLC has terminated its original $250M MassMutual-funded SPV lending facility after its three-year reinvestment period expired with zero outstanding borrowings, suggesting an orderly wind-down and rotation into newer, larger financing lines.

---

### C. What's New

- **Facility termination officially disclosed:** On April 3, 2023, SPV Facility I entered into the MassMutual SPV I Facility with Massachusetts Mutual Life Insurance Company as administrative agent and facility servicer. That agreement — together with all related loan documents — has now been formally terminated via a Termination Agreement executed April 6, 2026.

- **Zero-balance exit confirmed:** Per the 8-K, prior to the reinvestment period expiration on April 3, 2026, SPV Facility I had **no outstanding borrowings** under the MassMutual SPV I Facility — a significant departure from recent usage patterns. For the three and six months ended June 30, 2025, the daily average amount of outstanding borrowings under the MassMutual SPV I Facility were $187,500,000 and $190,074,586, respectively. The fund clearly drew down and repaid the facility entirely before the reinvestment period closed.

- **All security interests and liens released:** The 8-K states that upon execution of the Termination Agreement, all security interests and liens in favor of any secured party, and all obligations thereunder, were released and terminated. This constitutes a clean lien release on the SPV's asset pool.

- **Named servicer newly spotlighted:** The filing identifies **Barings Finance LLC** as administrative agent and facility servicer — a detail not prominently surfaced in prior coverage. Barings Finance LLC is a subsidiary of MassMutual, making this a vertically integrated insurance-capital-to-private-credit structure that is now fully unwound.

- **Facility size had been expanded:** On September 26, 2023, SPV Facility I and MassMutual amended the MassMutual SPV I Facility, increasing the aggregate commitments by the lenders to $250,000,000. The termination thus retires a facility that had grown from $200M to $250M before being wound down.

- **Natural lifecycle, not distress-driven:** The trigger was the scheduled reinvestment period expiration date of April 3, 2026, after which no additional borrowings were permitted — consistent with standard CLO/SPV facility structuring.

---

### D. Most Important Points

- **Terminated facility size:** $250M commitment (amended up from $200M in September 2023). Now fully retired. No successor SPV Facility I arrangement announced.

- **Lenders were insurance companies:** Massachusetts Mutual Life Insurance Company and Massachusetts Ascend Life Insurance Company were the sole named lenders — not banks or traditional private credit funds. This is insurance capital deployed into a BDC leverage structure.

- **Barings Finance LLC as servicer/agent:** Massachusetts Mutual Life Insurance Company acted as administrative agent and facility servicer. The 8-K names Barings Finance LLC in that agent/servicer role — a unit fully owned by MassMutual, illustrating MassMutual deploying capital through its own affiliated servicer into a third-party BDC. That chain is now severed.

- **Pricing terms (historical):** Borrowings under the MassMutual SPV I Facility generally bore interest at a rate per annum equal to Term SOFR plus a margin of 3.25%, with a 1.0% floor on Term SOFR.

- **Advance rate:** The MassMutual SPV I Facility had an advance rate of 58% against eligible portfolio assets.

- **Collateral structure:** The MassMutual SPV I Facility was secured by all of the assets of SPV Facility I and a pledge over 100% of the equity interest the Company holds in SPV Facility I.

- **Fund scale at termination:** StepStone Private Credit Fund LLC is conducting a private offering for up to $10 billion and has issued approximately 76,848,115 shares for $2,007.9 million to date. At $2B+ in equity raised, the $250M facility was a declining fraction of total capitalization.

- **Broader financing infrastructure remains intact:** SPCF retains at least a BMO revolving facility (SPV II), a Wells Fargo facility (SPV III, expanded to $400M in late 2024), and a new SPV Facility V originated July 2025. The lenders have made aggregate commitments of $400.0 million under the Wells Fargo SPV III Credit Facility.

- **StepStone Group fundraising context:** StepStone Group reported record $34 billion in fundraising, with a private wealth platform reaching $15 billion, driven by international institutions and a private wealth business generating more than $2 billion in subscriptions per quarter.

- **Reinvestment period discipline:** The fact that SPCF wound the borrowing balance to zero before the reinvestment period expired — rather than carrying residual balances into the tail period — is notable portfolio hygiene, suggesting active liability management rather than passive run-off.

---

### E. Why It Matters Now

This termination is most directly relevant to the **"banks expanding into private credit"** and **"insurance capital as private credit funder"** themes, though in reverse: the MassMutual-Barings Finance LLC lending structure to SPCF has been unwound, not expanded. Private debt fundraising remained healthy in 2025, with evergreen vehicles (e.g., BDCs) continuing to grow rapidly, broadening the investor base but reinforcing deployment pressure. SPCF's rotation away from the MassMutual facility toward newer, larger, bank-administered facilities (Wells Fargo at $400M, BMO) reflects a maturing BDC borrowing stack — routine for a growing fund — rather than any sign of stress. There is no evidence of redemption pressure, credit deterioration, or liquidity management distress in this filing. The zero-balance clean exit actually suggests strong cash management and disciplined liability lifecycle governance.

---

---

### G. Signals Reporters Should Notice

- **Barings Finance LLC's servicer role:** Barings is one of the largest insurance-owned private credit managers globally. Its role as facility servicer to a rival BDC (SPCF) — not just as a lender but as the operational agent — is an under-reported structural detail. Now terminated.

- **MassMutual as direct BDC lender:** MassMutual and its subsidiary Ascend deployed insurance capital directly into a BDC leverage facility. With that facility now retired, it is worth asking whether MassMutual is redeploying into similar structures elsewhere or pulling back from BDC-level leverage.

- **Zero borrowings before period expiry:** SPCF had ~$187–190M in daily average borrowings through mid-2025 but reached zero before the April 3, 2026 reinvestment deadline. The speed of paydown warrants attention — was this a deliberate de-risking given current credit market volatility, or routine portfolio turnover funded by the $2B equity raise?

- **Rapid BDC growth and facility evolution:** SPCF now has at least four SPV facilities (II through V), with the Wells Fargo SPV III at $400M — nearly double the retired MassMutual line. A Loan and Security Agreement dated July 25, 2025, was entered into for SPV Facility V. This proliferation of leverage structures in a growing BDC merits ongoing monitoring.

- **$10B private offering target vs. $2B raised:** SPCF is less than 21% toward its stated $10B fundraising target. The pace and sustainability of inflows into this vehicle — particularly in a risk-off environment — is a story worth tracking.

---

### H. Routine vs. Non-Routine

**Routine / Expected:**
- Facility terminates naturally at end of reinvestment period (3-year term from April 2023 to April 2026) — this is standard SPV/CLO lifecycle mechanics.
- Zero outstanding balance at termination is consistent with normal amortization/repayment as new facilities replaced the old one.
- Item 1.02 disclosure is the required form for material agreement termination — procedurally obligatory.
- Lien release and obligation discharge upon execution is boilerplate for a clean payoff.

**Potentially Non-Routine / Notable:**
- The identification of **Barings Finance LLC** as administrative agent and servicer (not just MassMutual itself) is a structural nuance worth flagging — insurance company using its affiliated credit manager as agent for its own lending is an integrated model that blurs the lines between insurance capital and private credit management.
- The rapid paydown from ~$187–190M average in H1 2025 to zero by April 2026 — a ~$190M reduction in under 12 months — is notable and may reflect deliberate liability management ahead of the reinvestment expiry.
- The concurrent existence of SPV Facility V (July 2025) suggests SPCF pre-built replacement capacity before retiring this line, which is financially disciplined but also raises questions about total leverage and lender diversity.

---

### I. Questions for Follow-Up

1. **Why did SPCF wind borrowings to zero by April 3, 2026?** Was this driven by portfolio paydowns, asset sales, or a deliberate decision to reduce leverage ahead of market uncertainty — or simply mechanical repayment as loans matured?

2. **Is MassMutual / Barings Finance redeploying this $250M insurance capital elsewhere in private credit?** This could signal a shift in MassMutual's appetite for BDC leverage financing.

3. **What is SPV Facility V (July 2025)?** Which bank or institution is serving as lender/agent, and what are the size and pricing terms? Is SPCF increasing total leverage capacity even as it retired this line?

4. **What is SPCF's current total leverage (debt-to-equity) across all SPV facilities?** With SPV II (BMO), SPV III (Wells Fargo, $400M), and SPV V all active, the aggregate leverage picture is opaque from this single filing.

5. **Has SPCF's portfolio composition shifted materially since 2023?** The initial portfolio was first lien, senior secured middle market loans acquired from an affiliated StepStone fund. Has sector concentration or credit quality changed as the fund has grown past $2B in equity?

6. **Is the $10B fundraising target still realistic given current private wealth market conditions?** StepStone's private wealth platform achieved $15 billion in platform AUM and over $2.2 billion in new subscriptions during the most recent quarter, but SPCF specifically is at $2B — are inflows accelerating or decelerating?

7. **What fees were paid on April 6, 2026 at termination?** The filing references "all remaining fees" but does not quantify the amount. A facility unused at termination would still incur non-use/commitment fees — the total could be material.

---

## SEC Filing Analysis: StepStone Private Credit Fund LLC — SC TO-I/A (Final Amendment), April 10, 2026

---

### A. Relevance Verdict

**HIGHLY RELEVANT TO PRIVATE CREDIT**

This is a final amendment to a tender offer by a semi-liquid private credit fund — a structure under intense industry scrutiny in early 2026. The zero-redemption result and the disclosed feeder fund offset mechanism both warrant reporter attention.

---

### B. One-Line Takeaway

StepStone's private credit fund reports zero net shares tendered in its Q1 2026 repurchase offer, citing a feeder fund's internal netting of subscription proceeds against repurchase requests — a structural footnote that deserves scrutiny given industrywide redemption pressure.

---

### C. What's New

- **Zero shares tendered and zero accepted.** The fund's tender offer for up to 3,580,981 shares, launched February 4, 2026 and expiring March 4, 2026, resulted in no redemptions whatsoever.
- **Feeder fund netting mechanism disclosed for the first time in this amendment.** The fund explicitly states the zero result is calculated "taking into account an existing Company feeder fund's normal course utilization of subscription proceeds to offset repurchase amounts in its own liquidity program prior to submitting any repurchase request." This internal offset mechanism is newly disclosed in this final amendment.
- **This is the final amendment (Amendment No. 1)** to the Schedule TO originally filed February 4, 2026 — confirming the offer is now formally closed with no payouts.
- **NAV pricing date confirmed as March 31, 2026.** The purchase price was to be set at NAV per share as of March 31, 2026 — this date is new and post-offer-expiry, suggesting NAV settlement mechanics extend beyond the tender window.
- **Signed by CFO Joseph Cambareri** rather than named CEO Darren Friedman — a minor but potentially notable change in signatory from prior filings.

---

### D. Most Important Points

- **Offer size: up to 3,580,981 shares** — at the fund's most recently disclosed NAV of $26.40/share (as of Feb. 28, 2026), that represents a maximum potential redemption pool of approximately **$94.5 million**. Zero was actually paid out.
- As of February 28, 2026, the fund's aggregate NAV was approximately **$2,038.4 million**, the fair value of its investment portfolio was approximately **$3,186.1 million**, and it had **$1,238.7 million in debt outstanding** (at principal).
- The fund is conducting a private offering for up to **$10 billion** and had issued **76,848,115 shares for $2,007.9 million** to date as of late March 2026.
- The feeder fund offset mechanism is key: a feeder fund first used **new subscription proceeds** to satisfy its own investors' repurchase requests before netting against the master fund's program — meaning underlying investor redemption demand at the feeder level may not be fully visible in this filing's headline zero figure.
- The fund is structured as a **tender offer fund** (not an interval fund), giving the board significant discretion on whether and how much to repurchase. Tender offer funds can issue redemptions at the discretion of their boards, with redemption periods ranging from quarterly to annual.
- Tender offer funds operate under a different regulatory framework than interval funds, one that grants fund managers the explicit ability to suspend, limit, or decline repurchase offers when doing so is determined to be in the best interest of the fund.
- The fund is a **Delaware LLC** issuing limited liability company interests, not registered shares — confirming its private placement / non-traded structure.
- Legal counsel: **Dechert LLP** (Richard Horowitz, Esq. and Clay Douglas, Esq.), a standard but high-profile private funds law firm.
- CEO is named as **Darren Friedman**; CFO and signatory here is **Joseph Cambareri**.
- The original Schedule TO was filed **February 4, 2026**; offer expiry was **March 4, 2026** — a standard ~30-day window.

---

### E. Why It Matters Now

This filing lands squarely in the middle of the most active redemption-pressure cycle in private credit history. Multiple redemption restrictions by private credit funds in early 2026 have generated widespread concerns and congressional attention regarding the risks of the nearly $2 trillion U.S. private credit market. Against that backdrop, StepStone reporting zero net redemptions could appear reassuring — but the feeder fund netting disclosure complicates that reading. Boaz Weinstein of Saba Capital has specifically flagged fund-of-funds-style structures, noting they have limited control over fulfilling their own redemption requests — and StepStone's feeder fund offset mechanism raises a structurally similar question: are investor redemption requests being absorbed at the feeder level and netted out before they ever formally reach the master fund? Meanwhile, private placement BDCs paid $1.2 billion in redemptions in Q1 2026, meeting only 74% of investor requests, making StepStone's zero figure either a genuine outlier or a product of structural design.

### G. Signals Reporters Should Notice

- **Feeder fund internal netting of subscription proceeds vs. redemptions** — this mechanism means gross redemption demand at the feeder level is invisible in the headline zero figure. The fund may be absorbing repurchase requests within the feeder before they reach the master fund's formal tender. This structural opacity is a direct echo of concerns raised about multi-layered private credit vehicles.
- **Zero redemptions during the single most active redemption quarter for the private credit industry** — either StepStone's investor base is uniquely stable, or the feeder fund netting is doing structural work. Reporters should probe which it is.
- **Tender offer fund structure** gives the board maximum discretion to decline or limit repurchases — BDCs and tender offer funds can gate redemptions if their boards approve it. This is a structurally different and less investor-protective mechanism than interval funds.
- The fund is conducting a private offering for up to $10 billion — continued fundraising at this scale, simultaneously with a zero-redemption result, raises the question of whether inflows are being used to manage liquidity rather than grow the portfolio.
- **Saba/Cox third-party tender offer risk** — Saba Capital and Cox Capital Management launched tender offers for stakes in Blue Owl nontraded private credit funds at a 34.9% discount. StepStone's fund, if experiencing suppressed-but-real redemption demand, could become a target for similar discount tender activity.

---

### H. Routine vs. Non-Routine

**Routine / expected:**
- Filing of final amendment (SC TO-I/A) to close out a completed tender offer cycle is a standard regulatory requirement for tender offer funds.
- 30-day offer window (Feb. 4 – March 4, 2026) is normal for this fund structure.
- Dechert LLP as counsel is standard for this type of vehicle.
- Delaware LLC structure and private placement format are boilerplate for this fund type.
- NAV pricing at quarter-end (March 31, 2026) is consistent with typical semi-liquid fund mechanics.

**Potentially non-routine / notable:**
- **Zero net redemptions during the highest-redemption quarter in the sector's history** is not routine and demands explanation.
- **Feeder fund subscription-proceeds-netting disclosure** is unusual and structurally significant — it suggests the zero headline result is a net figure, not a gross figure, and that the netting mechanism is "normal course" (suggesting it has been used before, not disclosed as prominently).
- The **$10 billion continuous private offering** running simultaneously with a zero-redemption outcome raises a question of whether new inflows are structurally supporting liquidity without being described as such.
- **CFO, not CEO, signing the final amendment** — minor, but potentially worth noting given CEO Darren Friedman is named in the filing header.

---

### I. Questions for Follow-Up

1. **What was the gross redemption demand at the feeder fund level before the netting mechanism was applied?** The zero headline figure is net — what is the gross?
2. **How does the feeder fund's subscription-proceeds-netting work mechanically?** Does it effectively allow new investors to fund existing investor exits without those exits being registered as redemptions at the master fund level?
3. **Has this feeder fund netting mechanism been disclosed in prior tender offer cycles?** If not, why is it appearing now for the first time?
4. **Is the $10 billion continuous private offering still actively raising capital, and are inflows being used to satisfy liquidity rather than make new investments?**
5. **What is the fund's current non-accrual rate, and have any portfolio company valuations been marked down recently?** The $3.19B portfolio vs. $2.04B NAV implies significant leverage at the portfolio level — are any underlying loans showing stress?
6. **Has StepStone's feeder fund structure attracted interest from discount tender offer players like Saba Capital or Cox Capital?**
7. Q1 2026 was the first time NAV BDCs had to prorate redemptions, according to Stanger — did StepStone receive any investor redemption requests at all, including those handled at the feeder level?
8. **What is the fund's redemption calendar for Q2 2026?** Given that redemption requests have outpaced repurchase mechanics across multiple large private credit interval funds, with deferred redemption queues expected to take several quarters to resolve, will StepStone expand or contract its next tender offer size?

---

### J. Evidence from the Filing

**Key passage (Final Results section of Amendment No. 1):**
> "No Shares were tendered by Shareholders in connection with the Offer (taking into account an existing Company feeder fund's normal course utilization of subscription proceeds to offset repurchase amounts in its own liquidity program prior to submitting any repurchase request in the Company's share repurchase program) and, as a result, the Company has accepted no Shares for purchase pursuant to the Offer."

- **Source:** SC TO-I/A body text, results reporting section.
- **Why it matters:** This is the only substantive new disclosure in the filing and contains the feeder fund netting language that is the key analytical issue. The parenthetical is doing enormous structural work — it converts what could be a non-zero gross redemption figure into a net-zero headline number.

**Original offer parameters (from Schedule TO cross-reference):**
- Offer size: up to **3,580,981 shares**
- Pricing: **NAV per share as of March 31, 2026**
- Offer launched: **February 4, 2026**
- Offer expired: **11:59 p.m. ET, March 4, 2026**

**Fund background (from related recent filings, not this document):**
- NAV per share as of February 28, 2026 was **$26.40**; aggregate NAV approximately $2,038.4 million; investment portfolio fair value approximately $3,186.1 million; debt outstanding $1,238.7 million.

---

### K. Final Newsroom Brief

StepStone Private Credit Fund LLC filed the final amendment to its Q1 2026 tender offer on April 10, reporting that **zero shares were tendered and zero were purchased** — a headline result that, on its face, suggests the fund faces no investor redemption pressure. However, buried in the filing is a critical structural disclosure: the zero result is calculated *after* a feeder fund used new subscription proceeds to internally offset its own investors' repurchase requests before those requests were ever formally submitted to the master fund's program. This feeder fund netting mechanism — described as "normal course" — means the headline figure obscures the true gross redemption demand investors sought, and reporters should press for that gross number. The disclosure is highly relevant given that multiple redemption restrictions by private credit funds in early 2026 have generated widespread concerns and congressional attention, and that private placement BDCs paid $1.2 billion in redemptions in Q1 2026, meeting only 74% of investor requests. StepStone's zero figure either reflects genuine investor satisfaction — plausible given the fund's still-active $10 billion continuous fundraise — or it reflects a structural design that routes redemption pressure through a feeder layer before it surfaces in regulatory filings. The uncertainty here is material: without the gross feeder-level demand figures, this filing cannot be taken at face value as evidence of no redemption stress.

## SEC Filing Analysis: StepStone (Luxembourg) SCA SICAV – StepStone Private Credit ELTIF | Form D, Filed April 9, 2026

---

### A. Relevance Verdict

**RELEVANT TO PRIVATE CREDIT**

This is a direct private credit fundraising/distribution filing from a named private credit manager, with implications for StepStone's European wealth-channel expansion strategy. No stress or distress signals are present, but the filing is meaningfully relevant to private credit market expansion themes.

---

### B. One-Line Takeaway

StepStone has filed a Form D with the SEC for its Luxembourg-domiciled Private Credit ELTIF, formally notifying U.S. regulators of a Rule 506(b) exempt offering, suggesting the fund is now being made available to U.S. qualified purchasers or institutional investors.

---

### C. What's New

- **New SEC registration footprint for a European structure:** StepStone launched the StepStone (Luxembourg) SCA SICAV – StepStone Private Credit ELTIF under the EU's updated ELTIF 2.0 fund regime in January 2025, but this Form D filed April 9, 2026 is a new SEC-side notification, indicating the fund is now being formally offered under U.S. securities law exemptions.

- **Dual-exemption structure claimed:** The filing asserts Rule 506(b), Investment Company Act Section 3(c), and Section 3(c)(7) exemptions simultaneously — suggesting the fund is targeting U.S. qualified purchasers and institutional counterparties, not solely European retail or professional investors.

- **Minimum investment set at $50,000:** This is a newly disclosed specific entry threshold for the ELTIF under the U.S. exemption framework — lower than many institutional private credit vehicles but higher than typical retail-facing interval funds.

- **Offering amount listed as Indefinite, total raised shown as $0:** The filing discloses no capital raised to date under this specific U.S. exemption, indicating this is either an initial notification or a new share class/compartment being opened for U.S.-connected investors.

- **Named AIFM newly identified in U.S. filing context:** StepStone Group Europe Alternative Investments Limited, based in Dublin, is formally named as the Alternative Investment Fund Manager (AIFM) of the issuer — the first time this role has been disclosed in a U.S. Form D for this fund.

- **U.S.-based director on Luxembourg fund board:** Timothy A. Smith, listed c/o StepStone Group Private Wealth LLC in Charlotte, NC, is named as a manager of the Board of the General Partner — signaling a deliberate bridge between the European fund structure and StepStone's U.S. private wealth distribution operation.

---

### D. Most Important Points

- **Fund structure:** Luxembourg SCA SICAV structured as a "Compartment of a Luxembourg investment company," with StepStone (Luxembourg) GP S.à r.l. as General Partner and StepStone Group Europe Alternative Investments Limited (Dublin) as AIFM.

- **Regulatory exemptions claimed:** Rule 506(b) private placement, Investment Company Act Section 3(c) and Section 3(c)(7) — the 3(c)(7) exemption restricts sales to "qualified purchasers," typically institutions or very high-net-worth individuals with $5M+ in investments.

- **Minimum investment: $50,000.** This is below typical institutional thresholds and suggests the fund may be targeting semi-professional or high-net-worth individuals through U.S. wealth channels, consistent with StepStone's broader private wealth push.

- **Total offering: Indefinite; amount raised: $0 under this filing.** This is a new or fresh U.S. filing — no capital has yet been raised under this specific exemption tranche.

- **ELTIF 2.0 framework:** The ELTIF 2.0 fund regime opens up wider opportunities for asset managers to offer a purpose-built entry point for European investors in illiquid assets. This filing extends that access toward U.S. regulatory cover.

- **Targeted geographies for ELTIF marketing:** StepStone plans to initially market ELTIFs in Italy, Spain, Germany, France, and the Nordic and Benelux regions, focusing on investing in private credit assets in the European Union.

- **Platform and AUM context:** As of December 31, 2025, StepStone was responsible for approximately $811 billion of total capital, including $220 billion of assets under management.

- **Fundraising momentum:** StepStone Group pulled in more than $34 billion in gross asset additions over the past 12 months — its best fundraising stretch ever — fueled by international institutions and a private wealth business that now generates more than $2 billion in subscriptions per quarter.

- **AIFM fee:** Disclosed as payable to StepStone Group Europe Alternative Investments Limited, with terms referenced to offering materials only — no specific rate or structure disclosed in this filing.

- **Signing authority:** The Form D was signed by Christian Hinze (Luxembourg) and Timothy A. Smith (Charlotte, NC), underscoring the hybrid European/U.S. governance design.

---

### E. Why It Matters Now

StepStone received regulatory approval to launch a Private Debt-based ELTIF in February 2025, as part of its continued expansion into the European private wealth market. This Form D represents a further evolution of that strategy — StepStone is now formally extending this Luxembourg vehicle into the U.S. regulatory perimeter, likely to allow U.S. qualified purchasers or globally distributed wealth platforms to access the fund. This is a clean example of the aggressive geographic and channel expansion currently characterizing the private credit fundraising landscape. There are no stress, default, or liquidity signals in this filing — the relevance is entirely on the fundraising expansion and distribution theme. Reporters covering the democratization of private credit or the transatlantic push by private debt managers should take note, but this is not a distress signal.

- **Zero capital raised under this exemption:** This is the filing's opening shot — no U.S. capital has yet been raised. Watch for amended Form D filings that will show actual subscription data. First close figures will be a newsworthy data point.

Smith of StepStone Group Private Wealth LLC in Charlotte serves on the Luxembourg fund's Board, directly linking the ELTIF to StepStone's U.S. private wealth distribution infrastructure. - **AIFM fee terms withheld:** Fee disclosures are deferred entirely to offering materials. Reporters should request the offering memorandum to check fee levels relative to comparable U.S. private credit interval funds or BDCs.

---

### H. Routine vs. Non-Routine

**Routine / Expected:**
- Form D is standard notification for Regulation D private placements; no unusual procedural elements.
- Luxembourg SCA SICAV fund structure with a Luxembourg GP and EU AIFM is standard for ELTIF vehicles.
- AIFM fee disclosed by reference to offering materials only — typical for Form D filings.
- Indefinite offering size is common for evergreen or perpetual private credit vehicles.
- Dual 3(c)/3(c)(7) exemption claims are standard for private funds targeting U.S. institutions.

**Potentially Non-Routine / Notable:**
- A Luxembourg ELTIF filing a Form D with the SEC is structurally uncommon — ELTIFs are typically European-only vehicles; the 506(b)/3(c)(7) layer suggests active outreach to U.S.-based qualified purchasers that may not have been previously publicized.
- The $50,000 minimum is lower than many private credit vehicles using 3(c)(7), raising questions about whether the target investor profile has evolved since the fund's January 2025 launch.
- Zero reported capital raised under the U.S. exemption, despite the fund having been operational since January 2025 — suggests the U.S. distribution push is only just beginning.
- Timothy A. Smith's dual role (U.S. private wealth + Luxembourg board seat) is an organizational design choice that links institutional and wealth-channel distribution directly.

---

### I. Questions for Follow-Up

1. **Who exactly are the targeted U.S. investors?** The 3(c)(7) exemption requires qualified purchasers — are these U.S. family offices, pension funds, or wealth-channel platforms? Does this contradict the ELTIF's stated European retail mandate?

2. **Has the fund already raised capital in Europe under ELTIF 2.0 rules?** If yes, how much and from which investor types? The $0 reported in this Form D covers only the U.S. exemption tranche — the European side is not reflected.

3. **What are the redemption terms for the ELTIF?** ELTIF 2.0 introduced some liquidity provisions, but illiquidity is central to the structure. Do the U.S. tranche terms differ from what European investors are offered?

4. **What is the AIFM fee structure?** Is it comparable to U.S. BDC or interval fund fee levels? Any performance fee or carried interest disclosed in the offering memorandum?

5. **Why file now, 15 months after the January 2025 fund launch?** Was the U.S. tranche always planned, or is this a strategic pivot following strong European fundraising?

6. **Which U.S. wealth platforms, if any, will distribute this fund?** StepStone's CRDEX is already on CrowdStreet and other platforms — is the ELTIF intended for different channels?

7. **How does the $50,000 minimum compare to the European minimum investment threshold** under the specific ELTIF 2.0 offering? Is there regulatory arbitrage between the EU and U.S. sides?

### J. Evidence from the Filing

- **Exemptions claimed (Form D header fields):** Rule 506(b); Investment Company Act Section 3(c); Section 3(c)(7) — all three checked as applicable. Section 3(c)(7) restricts participation to "qualified purchasers."

- **Fund type field:** "Pooled Investment Fund / Other Investment Fund" — not a BDC, not a registered investment company under the 1940 Act.

- **Governance structure:** General Partner is "StepStone (Luxembourg) GP S.à r.l." at 10 rue du Chateau d'Eau, Leudelange, Luxembourg. AIFM is "StepStone Group Europe Alternative Investments Limited," 22–24 Lower Mount Street, Dublin 2, Ireland.

- **Minimum offering amount:** $50,000; Total offering size: "Indefinite."

- **Total amount sold:** 0 (all four numeric fields listed as zero) — this is a fresh U.S. regulatory notice with no capital reported.

- **AIFM fee disclosure:** "The AIFM is entitled to receive a fee for its services, as outlined in the Issuer's offering material" — terms deferred entirely to the private OM.

- **Organizational note:** Described as "Compartment of a Luxembourg investment company" — indicating this ELTIF is a sub-fund of the broader StepStone Luxembourg SCA SICAV umbrella, which also houses other StepStone private markets sub-funds.

- **Signing block:** "Christian Hinze and Tim Smith / Manager of the Board of Managers of the General Partner / 2026-04-09" — dual signatures from both Luxembourg and U.S.-domiciled managers.

### K. Final Newsroom Brief

StepStone Group has filed a Form D with the SEC on April 9, 2026, formally notifying U.S. regulators of a private offering by its Luxembourg-domiciled StepStone Private Credit ELTIF, invoking Rule 506(b) and the Investment Company Act's Section 3(c)(7) "qualified purchaser" exemptions. **What's new** is that this filing extends the European ELTIF into the U.S. regulatory perimeter for the first time, despite the fund having launched under ELTIF 2.0 rules in January 2025; no capital has yet been raised under this U.S. exemption. **Why it matters** is that it signals StepStone is systematically bridging its European private credit fund to U.S. qualified purchasers — likely family offices or wealth-channel institutions — consistent with the firm's record $34 billion fundraising year and its private wealth platform surpassing $2 billion in quarterly subscriptions. This fits squarely within the current theme of private credit managers aggressively expanding distribution across geographies and investor channels, using novel regulatory structures. **Key uncertainty:** The offering memorandum is not public, so fee terms, redemption conditions, and the full target investor profile remain opaque; reporters should seek the OM and clarify whether U.S. investor access is a strategic expansion or a technical regulatory housekeeping step.

This is a BDC that operates entirely as a direct private lender. The filing discloses Q1 2026 origination activity, portfolio composition, and two specific new commitments. No material stress signals surface, but the sharp quarter-over-quarter slowdown in new commitments and the tech-adjacent borrower warrant attention.

---

### B. One-Line Takeaway

MSC Income Fund originated $38.9 million in new/increased private loan commitments and funded $54.8 million in Q1 2026 — a steep sequential decline from Q4 2025, with a notable new DoD software/analytics deal as the headline transaction.

---

### C. What's New

- **New DoD software borrower:** $17.5 million in a first lien senior secured term loan, $2.5 million in a first lien senior secured revolver, and $5.0 million in a first lien senior secured delayed draw term loan to a provider of predictive analytics solutions to the U.S. Department of Defense, focusing on supply chain and maintenance applications. Total new commitment: **$25.0 million** across three tranches to a single, unnamed borrower.

- **New aviation ground-services follow-on:** Increased commitment of $5.9 million in an incremental first lien senior secured term loan to a provider of ground services to commercial, general and cargo aviation markets.

- **Portfolio size update:** As of March 31, 2026, MSC Income's private loan portfolio included total investments at cost of approximately $843.1 million across 80 unique companies. This compares to $821.7 million across 81 companies at December 31, 2025 — net growth of ~$21.4 million at cost, but the portfolio lost a net one borrower (exits/repayments exceeded new additions by count).

- **Portfolio composition confirmed:** The private loan portfolio, as a percentage of cost, included 92.6% invested in first lien senior secured debt investments and 7.4% invested in equity investments or other securities. First-lien concentration ticked up from 92.1% at year-end 2025.

- **Sharp origination slowdown vs. Q4 2025:** Q1 2026 new/increased commitments of $38.9 million compare to $131.8 million in Q4 2025, and funded investments of $54.8 million compare to $100.9 million in Q4 2025 — a roughly 70% and 46% drop, respectively, quarter-over-quarter.

- **Leverage capacity recently expanded:** On January 29, 2025, the Board approved the application of modified asset coverage requirements, reducing MSC Income Fund's asset coverage requirement applicable to senior securities from 200% to 150%, effective on January 29, 2026. This was a newly effective change as of Q1 2026 and expands the Fund's potential borrowing headroom.

---

### D. Most Important Points

1. **Q1 2026 origination volume is materially lower QoQ.** New/increased commitments dropped to $38.9M from $131.8M in Q4 2025; funded investments dropped to $54.8M from $100.9M. Not explained in the filing — likely a mix of deal timing and market conditions.

2. **Largest new commitment is a $25M three-tranche package to an unnamed DoD predictive analytics / supply-chain software company.** The $5M delayed draw component indicates the borrower has committed but not yet funded capital needs — an execution and drawdown risk to monitor.

3. **The aviation ground-services borrower is an incremental add-on, not a new relationship.** $5.9M incremental term loan — signals sponsor-backed follow-on activity but reveals the borrower needed additional capital.

4. **Portfolio shrank by one company net** (81 → 80), despite positive net dollar additions — at least one full exit or repayment occurred in Q1 but is not detailed in this filing.

5. **First-lien concentration at 92.6%** — marginally higher than Q4 2025's 92.1%, suggesting continued preference for senior-secured structures. Equity/other exposure at 7.4% is relatively low.

6. **Portfolio scale: $843.1M at cost across 80 borrowers** — average exposure per company of ~$10.5M. Consistent with the fund's stated investment range of $1 million to $30 million per private loan or LMM company.

7. **Fund is externally managed by MSC Adviser I, LLC** — a wholly-owned subsidiary of Main Street Capital Corporation. Conflict-of-interest risk between MSIF's interests and Main Street Capital's own portfolio is a standing structural consideration for reporters.

8. **Recent $150M notes offering (March 2026) provides dry powder.** MSC Income Fund closed a private notes offering totaling $150.0 million; the notes are unsecured, bear interest at a fixed rate of 6.34% per year, mature on May 31, 2029.

9. **BDC now publicly listed on NYSE (ticker: MSIF)**, having listed January 29, 2025 — meaning this is only the fifth full quarter of public disclosure. Price-to-NAV discount and liquidity dynamics are more visible than for non-listed BDCs.

10. **No defaults, non-accruals, or watchlist disclosures** in this filing. No covenant relief, PIK, or forbearance language. Filing presents a clean portfolio picture.

---

### E. Why It Matters Now

The filing is primarily a routine quarterly portfolio update but connects — modestly — to the **software/tech borrower risk** theme: the largest new Q1 commitment is a $25 million senior-secured package to an unnamed provider of predictive analytics and supply-chain software to the U.S. DoD. Software-to-government borrowers are less cyclically exposed than commercial SaaS, but the combination of a term loan, revolver, **and** delayed draw to a single unnamed borrower in the tech/analytics space is worth watching as BDCs have been under scrutiny for tech-sector underwriting. The broader filing does not show meaningful stress signals — no defaults, no non-accruals, no covenant amendments are mentioned. However, the sharp sequential decline in Q1 originations (down ~70% in new commitments QoQ) could be an early-cycle signal of deal activity cooling, consistent with broader private-credit market caution in early 2026. The newly effective 150% asset coverage ratio also gives MSIF expanded leverage room heading into a potentially tighter environment, raising the question of whether it will deploy capital aggressively at a time when underwriting standards are under scrutiny.

1. **Unnamed DoD software/analytics borrower receiving a $25M three-tranche commitment** — including a $5M delayed draw. The borrower's identity is not disclosed. Co-investment deals flow through the same adviser, raising allocation fairness questions when MSIF and MAIN compete for the same deals.

---

### H. Routine vs. Non-Routine

**Routine / Expected:**
- Quarterly 8-K portfolio activity announcement — standard disclosure cadence for a BDC
- First-lien senior secured structure on all disclosed deals — consistent with stated strategy
- Portfolio composition (92.6% first lien) in line with prior quarters
- Adviser relationship with Main Street Capital — longstanding, previously disclosed
- No defaults, non-accruals, or restructuring language — no stress signals

**Potentially Non-Routine / Notable:**
- Steep QoQ decline in origination activity (commitments down ~70%, funded down ~46%) — magnitude deserves explanation

---

### I. Questions for Follow-Up

1. **Who is the DoD predictive analytics borrower?** Government contract concentration, revenue profile, and PE sponsor should be disclosed to institutional investors — why is the name omitted?

2. **What drove the Q1 origination slowdown?** Is this seasonal deal timing, market caution post-tariff/macro volatility, or a deliberate pullback in deployment pace?

3. **Which company exited the portfolio** (portfolio went from 81 to 80 companies)? Was it a repayment, sale, or distressed exit?

4. **How is MSIF deploying its new 150% leverage capacity?** With the coverage ratio reduced effective January 2026, is leverage creeping up? The next 10-Q should show actual debt-to-equity levels.

5. **Is the aviation ground-services borrower a stressed follow-on?** An "increased commitment" to an existing borrower in a cyclically sensitive sector (commercial aviation services) could mean the company needed additional capital — or could be a routine tuck-in acquisition. Which is it?

7. **Is the 6.34% fixed-rate on the $150M unsecured notes adequately covered by the floating-rate loan book?** With rate cuts underway, the gap between the fund's fixed-rate liability costs and floating-rate asset income warrants scrutiny in the Q1 financial results.

> Fund mandate: The Fund is a principal investment firm that primarily provides debt capital to private companies owned by or in the process of being acquired by a private equity fund; portfolio investments are typically made to support leveraged buyouts, recapitalizations, growth financings, refinancings and acquisitions.

---

## A. Relevance Verdict

**LOW RELEVANCE** — This is a procedural Regulation FD disclosure announcing an earnings release date and conference call. It contains no new financial data, credit disclosures, portfolio updates, or material business developments.

---

## B. One-Line Takeaway

KBDC filed a routine 8-K under Reg FD to announce Q1 2026 results will be released May 11, 2026, with a conference call May 12; no new credit or portfolio information is disclosed.

---

- **Q1 2026 earnings release date confirmed:** May 11, 2026, after market close.

---

## D. Most Important Points

- **Form type:** 8-K, Items 7.01 (Reg FD) and 9.01 (Exhibits only). No financial statements filed.
- **Filer:** Kayne Anderson BDC, Inc. (NYSE: KBDC), externally managed by KA Credit Advisors, LLC, an indirect subsidiary of Kayne Anderson Capital Advisors, L.P.
- **Signing officer:** Terry A. Hart, CFO and Treasurer — signatory, not an unusual officer for this type of filing.
- **Strategy boilerplate restated:** The press release (Exhibit 99.1) reiterates KBDC's focus on first lien senior secured loans, unitranche, and split-lien loans to middle market companies — standard language, unchanged from prior filings.
- **No Q1 2026 data disclosed:** The filing explicitly defers all financial results to May 11, 2026.
- **Reg FD "furnished" designation:** The filing is "furnished," not "filed," under Section 18 of the Exchange Act — standard for Reg FD 8-Ks; limits legal liability.
- **Context from most recent prior results (Q4 2025, not in this filing):** KBDC reported Q4 2025 NII of $30.1 million, or $0.44 per share, with NAV of $16.32 per share and a debt-to-equity ratio of 1.02x. ---

## E. Why It Matters Now

This filing itself does not connect to any active private-credit stress theme. It is purely a calendaring disclosure. However, the **upcoming Q1 2026 earnings on May 11** are contextually important: KBDC enters Q1 2026 with a "value lending strategy" that management says deliberately avoids highly leveraged software loans, with approximately 2% of its portfolio in those sectors versus BDC peers with more than 20%. That positioning will be tested in the Q1 results given the broader private-credit debate around software/tech borrower risk and yield compression. Management specifically flagged that the strategy was designed to weather headwinds associated with software and tariffs. Q1 2026 will be the first hard data point since that framing.

Golub Capital BDC — which management called "planning for a challenging 2026" at its last earnings call amid lower rates, tighter spreads, rising non-accruals, and a dividend reset — has scheduled its fiscal Q2 2026 results for May 4, 2026, making this a key watch date for private-credit reporters.

- GBDC is managed by GC Advisors LLC, an affiliate of Golub Capital, which had **over $90 billion in capital under management** as of January 1, 2026.

---

## SEC Filing Analysis: Goldman Sachs Private Credit Corp. — SC TO-I/A, Filed April 6, 2026

---

### A. Relevance Verdict

**HIGHLY RELEVANT TO PRIVATE CREDIT**

This is a direct filing from a major non-traded BDC disclosing preliminary Q1 2026 tender offer results during an industry-wide redemption stress event. Goldman Sachs Private Credit Corp. is one of the most closely watched names in the non-traded private credit space, and this filing provides the first hard numbers on its Q1 redemption demand.

---

### B. One-Line Takeaway

Goldman Sachs Private Credit Corp.'s Q1 2026 tender offer received requests for 4.9990% of shares outstanding — essentially filling its entire 5% cap — but the fund honored 100% of requests, narrowly avoiding a gate.

---

### C. What's New

- **Preliminary Q1 2026 tender offer result disclosed for the first time:** 17,281,858 shares tendered, representing 4.9990% of shares outstanding as of December 31, 2025.
- **100% of tendered shares to be repurchased:** The fund confirmed it will accept all requests in full, without proration or gating.
- **Near-maximum utilization of the 5% cap:** The fund offered to repurchase up to 17,285,147 shares (5.0%); actual requests came in 3,289 shares short of the maximum — a razor-thin margin. This is functionally a cap-maxing event.
- **NAV pricing date now confirmed as March 31, 2026:** The price investors receive will reflect end-of-quarter NAV, which has not yet been finalized or disclosed publicly.
- **Final amendment still pending:** This is a preliminary result. A subsequent final amendment will disclose the exact dollar value of shares repurchased.
- **New exhibit filed (Q1 2026 Tender Offer Update):** Exhibit (a)(1)(vi) added; the content of this supplemental investor communication is not reproduced in the filing text excerpt provided.

---

### D. Most Important Points

- **Tender offer cap: 5.0% of shares outstanding** as of December 31, 2025 = up to 17,285,147 Class I shares.
- **Actual requests: 4.9990%** = 17,281,858 shares. The margin between requests and the fund's maximum repurchase capacity was just **3,289 shares** — effectively zero headroom.
- **All requests honored at 100%:** No proration, no gate. In the current market context, this is the headline Goldman will want told.
- **Pricing date: March 31, 2026 NAV.** End-of-quarter NAV has not yet been finalized; investors do not yet know the exact dollar amount they will receive.
- **Class I shares only** are subject to this offer; par value $0.001 per share. No other share classes mentioned.
- **Original tender offer filed March 2, 2026**; expiration was **11:59 p.m. ET, March 27, 2026**. This amendment is filed 10 days post-expiration.
- **Fund is managed by Goldman Sachs Asset Management, L.P.**, 200 West Street, New York, NY 10282.
- **Legal counsel:** Fried, Frank, Harris, Shriver & Jacobson LLP (New York) and Dechert LLP (Boston). Dual outside counsel on a routine tender offer amendment is standard for BDCs of this size.
- **Formerly named Goldman Sachs Private Credit Fund LLC** (May 2022) and before that **Goldman Sachs Loan Fund LLC** (March 2022), reflecting the BDC conversion history.
- **Signed by Stanley Matuszewski, CFO and Treasurer.** This is a management-level attestation, not a board resolution.

---

### E. Why It Matters Now

This filing lands at the center of the most-watched story in private credit right now: funds managed by Ares Management, Oaktree, and Goldman Sachs were among the last to update investors on the outcome of first-quarter tender offers at their private-credit funds. Goldman's Q1 result is now partially visible — and it is meaningfully different from peers. Apollo Global's $25 billion private credit fund capped redemptions at 5% of shares after investors sought to withdraw roughly 11.2% of total outstanding shares. Morgan Stanley limited redemptions at one of its private credit funds after investors sought to withdraw almost 11% of shares outstanding; its North Haven Private Income Fund returned roughly $169 million, or about 45.8% of investors' tender requests, for the quarter. By contrast, Goldman received requests for only 4.9990% — just barely under its 5.0% cap — and honored every dollar. That is a better outcome than most peers, but the near-maximum utilization of capacity is not comfort. Goldman's asset management arm had moved to reassure investors in a letter seen by Reuters in late February, disclosing that Goldman Sachs Private Credit Corp. posted a fourth-quarter redemption rate of 3.5%, well below the rate of more than 5% recorded by peers. The Q1 jump to ~5.0% is a material step-up from Q4's 3.5% and shows Goldman is not immune to the broader industry redemption trend, even if it avoided a gate this quarter.

### G. Signals Reporters Should Notice

- **Near-maxing of the 5% cap with just 3,289 shares of headroom** is not a clean outcome. It signals that redemption demand at Goldman came within a rounding error of triggering a gate — an important distinction from Goldman's own Q4 messaging of relative resilience.
- **Q1 redemption demand of ~5.0% is a sharp acceleration from Q4's 3.5%.** Goldman's asset management arm had disclosed a fourth-quarter redemption rate of 3.5%, well below the rate of more than 5% recorded by peers. The Q1 result nearly matches the peer levels Goldman was citing as a cautionary contrast.
- **Final March 31, 2026 NAV has not yet been disclosed.** In a quarter where JPMorgan re-marked loans with software exposure, the largest U.S. bank reduced the value of some loans to private-credit funds after reviewing the impact of market turmoil around software companies, going through its financing portfolio name by name and then sector by sector, and putting different marks on loans with underlying software exposure. Reporters should watch whether Goldman's Q1 NAV shows any markdown.
- **The "Q1 2026 Tender Offer Update" exhibit (a)(1)(vi)** is referenced but not reproduced in the filing text provided. This investor communication likely contains portfolio color, NAV context, or messaging about redemption trends. Reporters should pull the full exhibit from EDGAR.
- GS Credit's exposure to enterprise software credit stood at about 15.5% at end of the third quarter, which Goldman described as toward the low end of the range reported by competitors. With AI fears weighing on software borrowers and Q1 2026 NAV pending, that 15.5% exposure deserves renewed scrutiny.

---

### H. Routine vs. Non-Routine

**Routine / Expected:**
- SC TO-I/A amendment disclosing preliminary tender offer results is a standard procedural filing for non-traded BDCs.
- Industry standard redemption features for non-traded BDCs are quarterly share repurchases up to 5% of net asset value. Goldman's 5.0% cap is entirely standard.
- Pricing at quarter-end NAV is normal for this structure.
- Dual outside counsel (Fried Frank + Dechert) is routine for a BDC of this size.
- A follow-on final amendment to confirm exact share count and dollar amount is expected.

**Potentially Non-Routine / Notable:**
- Redemption requests of 4.9990% represent a near-maxing of the fund's repurchase capacity; Q4 2024 redemption rate was 3.5% — the Q1 2026 rate represents a significant step-up.
- The fund avoided a gate by a margin of just 3,289 shares. Any incremental investor tender request would have forced proration.
- The final March 31, 2026 NAV has not yet been set, leaving open the question of whether quarter-end markdowns will reduce the per-share payout.
- Goldman was among the last major private-credit fund managers to disclose Q1 tender offer results, raising questions about whether timing was deliberate.
- The filing includes a newly added investor communication exhibit (Q1 2026 Tender Offer Update) not previously filed, which may contain material qualitative disclosures.

---

### I. Questions for Follow-Up

1. **What does the Q1 2026 Tender Offer Update exhibit say?** Is Goldman offering any explanation for the redemption acceleration? Does it address software exposure, inflows, or NAV trajectory?
2. **What is the March 31, 2026 NAV per share?** Has Goldman marked down any positions in its portfolio relative to Q4 2025, particularly in software/tech? Did any markdowns drive incremental redemption requests?
3. **What were Q1 2026 gross inflows?** Goldman disclosed December inflows 11% above the year-to-date average, but the Q1 picture may have deteriorated. Is the fund in net inflow or net outflow for Q1 2026 on a combined basis?
4. **Is the near-maxing of the cap a trend or a one-off?** Q4 2024 redemption rate was 3.5%; Q1 2026 is ~5.0%. Is redemption demand accelerating quarter over quarter?
5. **How does Goldman's software/enterprise credit exposure look at March 31, 2026?** GS Credit's software credit exposure was ~15.5% at end of Q3 2024. Has that figure changed materially?
6. **Was this tender offer oversubscribed on a gross basis before any filtering?** The filing says 17,281,858 shares were "duly tendered" — how many were initially tendered before any deficiency letters or withdrawn tenders?
7. **What is the fund's current AUM and leverage ratio?** With redemptions at near-maximum capacity, how much dry powder does the fund have to honor future tenders without selling assets?
8. "Whether the BDC sector ultimately follows the same trajectory as non-listed REITs should become clearer over the coming months, as only four NAV BDCs have reported Q1 2026 tender offer results." Is Goldman's result the bellwether for the remaining large funds, and does Goldman plan any messaging to address broader investor concern?

---

### K. Final Newsroom Brief

Goldman Sachs Private Credit Corp. filed an amendment to its Q1 2026 tender offer statement on April 6, 2026, disclosing that investors tendered approximately 17.28 million Class I shares — representing 4.9990% of shares outstanding — essentially filling the fund's 5.0% quarterly repurchase cap with a margin of just 3,289 shares. The fund confirmed it will honor 100% of the requests at the March 31, 2026 NAV, which has not yet been finalized. What's new is the first hard data point on Q1 redemption demand at one of Goldman's flagship retail-oriented private credit vehicles, arriving weeks after peers including Apollo, Morgan Stanley, KKR, and Cliffwater disclosed far higher — and in several cases, gated — redemption requests. Goldman's Q4 redemption rate was just 3.5%, well below peers, making the near-maxing of the 5% cap in Q1 a notable deterioration, even if Goldman avoids the headline of a gate this quarter. The filing fits squarely within the current redemption-pressure theme gripping non-traded BDCs industry-wide, and the still-pending March 31 NAV — set against a backdrop of JPMorgan software loan re-markings and AI-driven credit concerns — means this story is not fully told; reporters should immediately pull the Q1 2026 Tender Offer Update exhibit from EDGAR and monitor the final amendment.

## SEC Filing Analysis: Barings Private Credit Corp — SC TO-I/A, April 6, 2026

---

### A. Relevance Verdict

**HIGHLY RELEVANT TO PRIVATE CREDIT**

This is a direct, documented instance of investor redemption pressure overwhelming a non-traded BDC's structural liquidity cap, with ~11% of shares tendered against a 5% maximum buyback limit.

---

### B. One-Line Takeaway

Barings Private Credit Corp confirmed its Q1 2026 tender offer was massively oversubscribed — investors sought to exit roughly 11% of shares outstanding, but the fund accepted only 5%, leaving more than half of redemption requests unfilled.

---

### C. What's New

- **Confirmed oversubscription at scale:** Barings accepted for purchase approximately 44.3% of shares validly tendered, meaning investors submitted roughly 2.26x the fund's maximum repurchase capacity.

- **Implied redemption demand of ~11.3% of shares outstanding:** The fund's 5% cap (6,974,335 shares) represented only 44.3% of what was tendered, implying total tender submissions of approximately 15.7 million shares — or roughly 11.3% of the December 31, 2025 share count. Bloomberg reported that about 11% of shares were requested.

- **Pro-rata proration disclosed for the first time in this amendment:** The original SC TO was filed March 2, 2026; this Amendment No. 1, filed April 6, 2026, is the first public disclosure of the oversubscription result and the pro-rata acceptance ratio.

- **NAV-based pricing confirmed as of March 31, 2026:** The purchase price was set at NAV per share as of the tender offer's expiration date — meaning price risk to redeeming investors was minimal, but remaining investors now hold a more concentrated position.

- **The fund hit its structural 5.0% buyback ceiling exactly:** The 6,974,335 shares accepted represent precisely 5.0% of total shares outstanding as of December 31, 2025, confirming the board exercised no discretion to expand capacity beyond the standard limit.

- **Peer comparator set newly named in offer materials:** The snippet discloses that the Offer to Purchase benchmarks Barings against Apollo Debt Solutions BDC, Ares Strategic Income Fund, Blackstone Private Credit Fund, Blue Owl Credit Income Corporation, and HPS Corporate Lending Fund — a useful competitive map for reporters.

---

### D. Most Important Points

- **Oversubscription ratio:** Only 44.3% of tendered shares were accepted on a pro-rata basis. Investors seeking full liquidity were denied more than half their requested redemptions.

- **Implied total tender demand:** ~11.3% of December 31, 2025 shares outstanding were submitted — more than double the 5% quarterly cap. Bloomberg confirmed the fund "is paying out less than half of the requests, capping withdrawals at 5%."

- **Structure:** Barings Private Credit Corporation is an externally managed, non-diversified, closed-end management investment company that has elected to be regulated as a BDC under the 1940 Act. It is a direct lending fund managed by Barings.

- **Standard liquidity mechanism triggered:** Non-traded funds like Barings Private Credit provide quarterly liquidity to investors through tender offers, typically capped at 5% of shares. That cap was reached in full here.

- **Pricing mechanism:** Purchase price equals NAV per share as of March 31, 2026 — an NAV-based exit, not a discounted secondary market transaction.

- **Co-CEO named:** Thomas Q. McDonnell is identified as the authorized officer. Legal counsel is Dechert LLP (Harry S. Pangas and Clay Douglas).

- **Fund formerly known as Barings Private Credit LLC**, incorporated April 2, 2021, converted to a Maryland corporation in May 2021.

- **No disclosure of asset sales, leverage draw, or affiliate backstop** to satisfy excess demand — unlike some peers (e.g., Oaktree Strategic Credit Fund, which used an affiliate promissory note to meet excess redemptions in Q1 2026).

- **Peer set disclosed for performance comparison:** Apollo Debt Solutions BDC, Ares Strategic Income Fund, Blackstone Private Credit Fund, Blue Owl Credit Income Corporation, HPS Corporate Lending Fund — all named in the Offer to Purchase as return benchmarks as of February 28, 2026.

- **Industry backdrop:** BDC redemptions increased across the board in Q4 2025; according to Cliffwater, redemptions in its index rose to 4.8% in Q4 2025 compared to 1.6% in Q3 2025.

---

### E. Why It Matters Now

Among BDCs with aggregate NAV of over $1 billion, redemptions rose by 217% quarter over quarter. The Barings result — with ~11% of shares tendered and only 5% accepted — is one of the most concrete Q1 2026 data points yet confirming that this redemption surge is not limited to Blue Owl or Blackstone. Assuming redemptions spike two to four times their quarterly limit in Q1 2026, analysts have estimated oversubscriptions could continue for a three to five quarter period. The Barings filing validates the top end of that range. Headline fears about default risk in the sector have driven a small but wealthy group of institutional investors to seek the exits from many of these funds, and this filing shows Barings investors are behaving identically. The absence of any affiliate backstop or expanded cap — unlike some peers — means unfilled redemptions are rolling forward, creating queued exit pressure that could persist across multiple quarters.

### G. Signals Reporters Should Notice

- **Severe oversubscription (2.26x capacity):** A 44.3% pro-rata fill rate means investor exit demand was more than twice what the fund's liquidity structure could accommodate — a strong behavioral signal, not a marginal one.

- **No discretionary capacity expansion:** Unlike Blackstone, which lifted quarterly redemption limits on its flagship BCRED fund from the usual 5% to 7.9% to meet rising investor demand, Barings enforced the hard 5% cap with no board override or affiliate purchase.

- **No affiliate backstop disclosed:** Oaktree Strategic Credit Fund disclosed that an affiliated entity purchased investor shares through a promissory note after its BDC received tender requests exceeding its quarterly repurchase limit during Q1 2026. Barings made no equivalent disclosure — unfilled shares may simply queue forward.

- **Queued redemptions create multi-quarter overhang:** To meet rising redemption requests, asset managers typically have two choices — either sell assets or borrow against their lines of credit. Barings has not disclosed which path, if any, it is pursuing.
